chip-blocks.description: The NTC thermistor (generic)'s function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). chip-circuit-divider.title: NTC thermistor (generic): Low-side divider
chip-circuit-divider.alt: Schematic of the NTC thermistor (generic) low-side divider: the chip with U2 MCU, R1 resistor 10 kΩ, C1 capacitor 100 nF; the MCU wires carry the port hooks ReadRaw().
chip-circuit-divider.description: A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected.

chip-outline.title: NTC thermistor (generic) package, 0603
chip-outline.alt: Outline of the NTC thermistor (generic) in 0603 drawn to scale from above: body 1.6 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm, 2 pins.
chip-outline.description: The NTC thermistor (generic) package seen from the top and, when the height is known, from the side, drawn to scale: 1.6 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm. The arrows carry the datasheet's dimensions, the dot marks pin 1 and the pads are numbered counter-clockwise from it, coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Pads sit centred on each side, evenly spaced; the datasheet's land pattern is the reference for a board.

chip-pinout.title: NTC thermistor (generic) pinout, 0603
chip-pinout.alt: Pinout of the NTC thermistor (generic) in 0603, top view: 2 pins, each with its name, its electrical type as a colour and the driver hook that uses it.
chip-pinout.description: The NTC thermistor (generic) seen from the top, in its 0603 package. Pin 1 is marked by the dot; the numbers run counter-clockwise from it. Each pad is coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Next to it is the pin's name and, in mono, the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it; a pin without a hook is not used by the driver.

conversion-pipeline.title: From an ADC code to a temperature
conversion-pipeline.alt: Pipeline of six stages: the mean of the samples, the classification of the code as open circuit, short circuit or out of scale, the divider's node ratio giving the resistance, the curve (table, Steinhart-Hart or beta) giving the temperature, the window and offset, and the uncertainty bound.
conversion-pipeline.description: Top to bottom, each arrow hands one number to the next stage. Read() takes sample_count codes and their mean (the spread check can stop it as Unstable). The mean code is classified: at or above 2^bits is CodeOutOfScale, a code in the margin at the open rail is OpenCircuit, one in the margin at the short rail is ShortCircuit; which rail is which depends on the divider side. The node ratio gives the thermistor's resistance from the series resistor, in 1/256 ohm. The resistance goes through the curve: a table (a bounded binary search, then linear interpolation in ln R) or Steinhart-Hart (a cubic in ln R) or the beta equation (1/T in Q32), any of them with no floating point and no library. The temperature must lie inside the window; the offset is added last. The uncertainty bound is computed from the same code. The stages are the functions of inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp.

driver-layers.title: The layers, one of them yours
driver-layers.alt: Layer diagram: your application calls the NtcThermistor core, which asks for ADC conversions through the ADC port contract to the port class you write, which reads the divider; the core and the contract are the same on every MCU.
driver-layers.description: Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers.
